analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' excess profits at 50% for two years and spends the proceeds on clean energy incentives.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee — no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor — so oil companies kept their tax breaks and their record profits went untaxed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged large oil companies a 50% fee on profits above their 2000–2004 average, while stripping them of several tax breaks and forcing renegotiation of cheap federal oil and gas leases. The money would fund a Strategic Energy Fund for clean energy research and biofuel projects. It also extended and expanded tax credits for solar, wind, biodiesel, ethanol, and fuel-efficient vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and energy consumers facing record 2006 gas prices, taxpayers who would benefit from oil companies contributing to a clean energy fund, and buyers of efficient homes and vehicles through extended tax credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise fee on the excess profits of integrated oil companies and large crude producers/refiners (over $100 million in gross receipts) for 2006 and 2007, with proceeds funding the Strategic Energy Fund [S2] [S3].

Eliminates several oil industry tax benefits — intangible drilling cost deductions, the domestic production deduction for oil and gas, geological and geophysical amortization, and favorable foreign tax credit rules — when oil prices exceed set thresholds [S2] [S3].
Directs the Interior Secretary to suspend royalty relief on federal lands when prices are high and to seek renegotiation of existing leases that lack price thresholds [S2] [S3].
Extends through 2014 tax credits for biodiesel, solar and fuel cell property, energy-efficient buildings and homes, and through 2017 the renewable electricity production credit [S2] [S3].

Creates new credits for making flexible-fuel and advanced-technology vehicles, investing in fuel-efficient fleets and small wind turbines, and captures carbon dioxide for enhanced oil recovery [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies and large crude producers and refiners, through the 50% excess profits fee, loss of tax deductions, a required inventory revaluation, and possible higher royalties on federal leases.

drawbacks.text: The 50% excess profits fee applies to producers and refiners, and a good-faith objection is that some of the cost could be passed along to consumers through higher prices at the pump — though prices were already at record highs [S2] [S3].
The bill required companies to retroactively revalue their oil inventories using a fixed $18.75-per-barrel formula for 2005, a one-time accounting change that reaches back to past tax years [S3].

Several incentives entrench existing beneficiaries: expanded ethanol producer credits and roughly $1 billion for cellulosic ethanol research flow to the biofuel industry, and new credits reward automakers for building flexible-fuel vehicles, which can still run entirely on gasoline [S2] [S3].
The excess profits fee applies only to tax years beginning in 2006 and 2007, making the revenue — and the clean energy spending it funds — temporary [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted money from record oil company profits to clean energy research and consumer-facing efficiency credits at a moment of high gas prices. The costs fall on a concentrated industry, and the main honest concerns are potential price pass-through to consumers and the retroactive inventory revaluation. On balance, the benefits for ordinary energy consumers and the revenue from windfall profits outweigh the drawbacks, though parts of the spending favor established biofuel and auto interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late May 2006, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Hillary Clinton introduced the bill in the Senate on May 23, 2006, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 28, 2006; the Finance Committee took no action on the bill for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies and large crude producers kept their tax deductions, royalty relief, and record profits; no consumer or clean energy program gained anything.

for.name: Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by a Republican in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show where parties stood; its only sponsor was a Democrat and it attracted zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.industry: Integrated oil companies and large crude producers/refiners
industries.note: The bill hit them directly: a 50% fee on excess profits, loss of drilling and domestic production tax deductions, restricted foreign tax credits, a forced inventory revaluation, and renegotiated federal leases. Its interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers paying record pump prices.

The bill extended biodiesel credits through 2014, doubled the small ethanol producer credit for sucrose and cellulos ethanol, and earmarked at least $1 billion for cellulosic ethanol commercialization. These incentives support lower-carbon fuels but lock in taxpayer support for the biofuel industry.

New credits would pay manufacturers up to $150 per flexible-fuel vehicle and 35% of investment in advanced-technology vehicle production, but flexible-fuel vehicles can run on ordinary gasoline, so the credit does not guarantee lower oil use.
Extended investment and production tax credits through 2014–2017 and added a residential small wind credit, reducing costs for clean electricity that competes with fossil generation.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands
industries.note: Royalty relief would be suspended when prices exceeded roughly $35 per barrel and existing leases renegotiated, returning value to taxpayers from publicly owned resources.
